chunks: "An operating system is the software layer that manages the hardware resources and lets application code share them. It sits between the programs and the hardware.

Its main jobs are: scheduling, deciding which task or process gets the CPU and when; memory management, giving each program memory and, on bigger systems, protecting programs from each other; device and I/O management through drivers, so an application can open a file or a socket without knowing the details of the flash chip or the Ethernet controller; and tools for tasks to communicate and synchronise, like queues, semaphores and mutexes.
On a PC or phone, that means Windows, Linux, Android.

On a microcontroller, it's usually a much smaller real-time operating system, like FreeRTOS or Zephyr, which might only provide the scheduler, a few synchronisation primitives and timers, in a few kilobytes of flash.
The alternative is bare-metal, where my code runs directly on the hardware with a main loop and interrupts.
An OS adds overhead in memory and CPU time, but it makes it much easier to run several activities with different timing at once, and to reuse drivers and libraries."
